    #85085. Tech Report: AI is changing software engineering — and some developers miss the struggle

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (951 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: AI is changing software engineering — and some developers miss the struggle

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (951 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that when Gemma Rodgers began her computer science degree in 2002, software engineering was seen as a future-proof and lucrative career.
    • It's an industry that has always moved fast, Rodgers, a software developer based in the U.K., told CNBC.
    • According to recent reports, as AI coding tools help engineers write, debug and test code faster than ever, some are mourning the job they used to have.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that when Gemma Rodgers began her computer science degree in 2002, software engineering was seen as a future-proof and lucrative career. It appealed to people who enjoyed getting into the weeds of code, tracking down bugs and building programs from scratch.

    It's an industry that has always moved fast, Rodgers, a software developer based in the U.K., told CNBC. But the arrival of artificial intelligence has accelerated the pace, with AI tools now part of the daily work of every software engineer she knows. In a 2026 Stack Overflow survey, 83% of software developer respondents said they use at least one AI tool.

    According to recent reports, as AI coding tools help engineers write, debug and test code faster than ever, some are mourning the job they used to have. Rodgers has always loved the sense of accomplishment that comes from piecing together different parts of code to find a solution, particularly when she's spent days, or even weeks, trying to fix a stubborn bug.

    "The sense of joy and fun that I used to experience by having a challenge and then having to work that out, it's been removed somewhat," she said. "Now you can sometimes do it in a few prompts, and it's great — but it's a breadcrumb of joy, not a full meal of joy.".

    In a recent development, rodgers is not alone in feeling nostalgic about the not-so-old days. Software engineers have taken to social media to describe missing their old way of working, when they could get into a flow state with code for hours at a time.

    Still, AI tools can be useful and have lowered the barrier to entry significantly. "It's becoming an industry where a lot of people have been able to thrive who wouldn't necessarily have been able to thrive 10 years ago, five years ago, even three years ago," Rodgers remarked.

    It's also crucial that the core skills engineers have traditionally learned on the job are not lost, she said. AI tools and internet services can go down unexpectedly, and engineers still need to know how to investigate problems and work through solutions themselves.

    "The sorts of skills that we were taught years ago are kind of being lost because [engineers are] having to just churn work out," Rodgers added.

    The job itself is changing, too. James Broadhead, chief technology officer of AI decision-making company Taktile, told CNBC that engineers who might previously have spent three weeks building a prototype can now generate 10 in an afternoon. The hardest part of that, he said, is "having the judgment to decide which of those are any good.".

    "The [AI] agents are spitting out so much code that [engineers] haven't read it all anymore," Broadhead mentioned. "It used to be you'd build up a sense of comfort and awareness of how the whole code base was structured, but now the whole thing changes all the time.".

    Joshua Wöhle, CEO of London-based AI training firm Mindstone, told CNBC he sees a growing divide between workers who know how to use AI effectively and those who don't.

    Sources indicate that the industry used to talk about "10X engineers," he remarked, who were dramatically more productive than their peers. Now, AI is widening that gap even further to produce "100X engineers.".

    Wöhle believes companies will increasingly have to decide whether to help employees catch up with AI or prioritize those who can get the most out of it. But he also understands why some engineers might struggle to adapt.

    The people who once excelled at the job were often those who loved writing and working through code, he mentioned, and those are not necessarily the current top performers.

    In a recent development, "That's the grief that is very, very real," Wöhle stated. "The thing you love doing is no longer the thing the organization should be paying for, to a degree, because it's no longer adding the value to the company that it used to.".

    But not every engineer sees the move away from hands-on coding as a bad thing. Chris Sees, a software engineer of more than 20 years and CEO of London-based virtual office firm Hoxton Mix, told CNBC that AI gives developers more time to tackle interesting problems. He views AI as a capable junior engineer that still needs supervision.

    It has been revealed that "The crucial thing is knowing what to delegate and when human judgement is needed," Sees said. "We'd be silly to think AI gets everything right, and I know I get a lot of satisfaction out of proving and spotting where it has gone wrong.".

    Even so, Sees worries about what happens to the next generation of engineers if AI takes over the routine coding and debugging through which they traditionally learned. Those tasks are "where you learn lessons and build scar tissue," he noted, and companies need to make sure AI becomes part of the learning process, rather than a shortcut.

    Sources indicate that for Rodgers, what matters is having control over how she uses the technology. As a self-employed developer, she can use AI to automate the parts of a project she finds tedious, while keeping the more interesting problem-solving for herself.

    She believes there's something vital about working through a difficult problem rather than immediately outsourcing it to technology. Friction and discomfort, she mentioned, are vital parts of the human experience.

    "As humans, we need to feel accomplished in something and part of accomplishment requires challenge," she stated. "Unless we are able to work that through in so many different aspects of life, then you never get the full force of the good feeling on the other side.".

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    Europe's cyber weak spot is the everyday businesses nobody thought to protect

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1027 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that cyberattacks on refrigerators in French supermarkets in October spurred Swedish chain Coop to act.
    • It has been revealed that attackers hit refrigeration systems in seven of its stores in early November.
    • Mundane but essential equipment, used by everyday businesses, has become a favorite target of cyber saboteurs in recent weeks.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that cyberattacks on refrigerators in French supermarkets in October spurred Swedish chain Coop to act. But it wasn't fast enough.

    It has been revealed that attackers hit refrigeration systems in seven of its stores in early November. The affected stores had been scheduled for security upgrades just two days later, a firm spokesperson told CNBC.

    Mundane but essential equipment, used by everyday businesses, has become a favorite target of cyber saboteurs in recent weeks.

    Experts are warning that a combination of known vulnerabilities, basic security failures and ambiguity over whether suppliers or their clients are responsible are making things worse, as AI makes cyber threats faster and more sophisticated.

    Guy Segal, CEO of cybersecurity firm Sygnia, told CNBC that his tech giant handled 285% more incidents in October than a year earlier, with demand forcing it to turn away some businesses seeking emergency assistance.

    "It's going to get worse before it's going to get better," Segal noted.

    The recent cyberattacks targeted refrigeration systems across hundreds of European supermarkets, remotely altering temperature settings and forcing retailers to discard spoiled food.

    France has since accused a cyber unit with links to Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps of the attacks, an allegation Tehran denies.

    Fredrik Blix, a cybersecurity researcher at Stockholm University, told CNBC that thousands of industrial control systems remain accessible over the public internet, sometimes despite manufacturers' warnings.

    Segal stated that basic cyber protection measures such as multi-factor authentication and basic network segmentation are more key than ever.

    He said risks to major civic infrastructure like the electrical grid were front of mind and so "usually pretty well protected.".

    Sources indicate that "There are always those civil supply chain components that are way, way less protected. Could be supermarkets, could be gas stations, could be… the screens on the Tube," Segal said, referring to London's underground rail system.

    The supermarket attacks demonstrated "this is the new normal, and definitely it's a wake-up call for every company out there," Segal added.

    According to recent reports, segal noted that inexpensive AI tools mean technical expertise and resources are no longer needed to launch attacks. He described one recent incident in which clients suffered breaches within six hours of a vulnerability becoming known, as perpetrators used AI to act faster — a process that might have taken weeks a year earlier.

    Segal, whose firm helps companies respond to breaches and strengthen their defenses, warned that businesses without prearranged incident-response support could struggle to secure emergency assistance, as overwhelmed cybersecurity firms prioritize existing clients.

    Recent findings suggest that in one case, he stated, Sygnia had to turn down a company because no response teams were available. Segal added that the company in question had already been turned down by ten other providers.

    Jacob Silverman, CEO of risk advisory firm Kroll, told CNBC earlier this month that the manufacturer was operating at full capacity in its incident-response business amid what he described as "the most rapid uptick in threat activity that we've ever seen.".

    Segal argued that retailers should treat cybersecurity risks with the same seriousness as fire safety and food hygiene, including when outsourcing maintenance.

    According to recent reports, when Ahold Delhaize stores in Belgium and Luxembourg were attacked on Nov. 2, it exposed how different independent store operators had responded to the warnings following the earlier attacks in France.

    Retailers had been warned about the vulnerabilities following earlier attacks in France, and those that implemented the recommended protections were spared, CEO Frans Muller told investors in an earnings call earlier this month, but smaller operators with fewer technical resources had struggled to make the necessary changes.

    Coop, whose stores are owned by regional consumer cooperatives or operated by franchises, told CNBC that public attention on the recent attacks was the main driver of security improvements. It said the vulnerability at the affected stores had since been addressed.

    The financial consequences of cyberattacks can be substantial. Ahold Delhaize told investors in November that a separate October cyberattack on its online operations and supply chain would reduce fourth-quarter sales by 200 million euros ($219 million).

    Danish shipping giant Maersk, which suffered an estimated $250 million to $300 million in losses from the 2017 NotPetya cyberattack, has spent nearly a decade strengthening its defenses.

    CEO Vincent Clerc told CNBC earlier this month that the experience had prompted significant investment in security capabilities, but warned that AI was enabling attackers to become more effective.

    "Everybody is in a race" to boost defenses, he stated.

    Research by cybersecurity firm Censys found that the number of internet-exposed refrigeration controllers made by Danfoss and Copeland exposed to cyber hacking fell 53% globally between Oct. 9 and Nov. 5.

    However, more than 3,100 remained exposed, and Censys said it could not determine whether the decline reflected permanent security improvements or equipment simply being taken offline.

    A Copeland spokesperson confirmed that some of its refrigeration systems were affected by the vulnerability and said it had contacted customers to reinforce cybersecurity guidance, including keeping devices off the public internet and updating software.

    Danfoss didn't respond to CNBC requests for comment.

    In a recent development, in the U.K., a covert cybersecurity operation has been underway to protect tens of thousands of refrigeration systems at supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants and other businesses, the BBC reported on Friday. After researchers discovered a major vulnerability in late October, cybersecurity specialists, IT teams and the U.K.'s National Cyber Security Centre worked to alert dozens of companies and secure their systems before hackers could exploit the flaw.

    The EU's Cyber Resilience Act will also impose stricter security requirements on manufacturers of connected products from December 2027.

    But the legislation does not require all existing equipment to be made compliant with the new standards.

    According to recent reports, blix told CNBC on Nov. 6 that European authorities should take a more proactive approach to reducing vulnerabilities by identifying exposed industrial control systems and contacting their operators before attacks occur.

    "What worries me is that we don't really do anything," he said, adding that "we are shuffling a lot of papers" and "doing a lot of risk assessments" but failing to take meaningful action.

    So much for buying the dip.As the S&P 500 entered correction territory and the Nasdaq-100 flirted with bear-market territory, down 19% from highs as of midday Friday, the single biggest options trade of the day was a near $100-million bet that the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) has a long way more to fall.Around 12:30 E.T., someone spent $93 million buying 20,000 380-strike puts expiring Sep. 17, 2027, according to trading data reviewed by SpotGamma and Volland, options-analytics platforms that both show the trade as a likely opening position, with volume exceeding existing open interest in the contract. The trade bets that the index will fall below $380, a nearly 8% decline from its current level. The SMH is off 40% from its recent all-time highs.

    "That trade stands out substantial-time," wrote Jason DeLorenzo, founder and owner of Volland. "It is either a hedge or speculative, but either way it isn't a vote of confidence."The puts were bought for $46.50 a piece, an arguably expensive choice for a downside bet with volatility in the ETF trading at 70.

    "You're paying a metric ton of Vega for that thing," added SpotGamma's Brent Kochuba, referring to the contract's sensitivity to changes in volatility of the underlying chip ETF. "Maybe they were a forced buyer, or maybe they're actually selling this, which can still be the case even though the price demonstrates it happening closer to the ask.".

    The semiconductor index headed for a 9% drop this week alone.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Tokenization platform Securitize climbed about 10% postmarket after reporting third quarter growth alongside increased operating expenses, and announcing an expansion into asset-backed finance through a strategic acquisition.
    • It has been revealed that miami-based Securitize, which made its public market debut in July, operates in the relatively new corner of the crypto equity universe involved in institutional tokenization infrastructure.
    • The growth came as bullish sentiment around tokenization gained traction throughout the third quarter, ahead of the Security and Exchange Commission formalizing the long awaited Innovation Exemption on Sept.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Tokenization platform Securitize climbed about 10% postmarket after reporting third quarter growth alongside increased operating expenses, and announcing an expansion into asset-backed finance through a strategic acquisition.

    It has been revealed that miami-based Securitize, which made its public market debut in July, operates in the relatively new corner of the crypto equity universe involved in institutional tokenization infrastructure. Tokenized assets on the platform grew 9% in the third quarter, to $4.8 billion, from the same period a year ago. Aggregate transaction volume rose 20% from a year ago, to $4.3 billion. Revenue of $11.5 million was up 28% from last year.

    The growth came as bullish sentiment around tokenization gained traction throughout the third quarter, ahead of the Security and Exchange Commission formalizing the long awaited Innovation Exemption on Sept. 17, which created a temporary pathway for trading of certain tokenized stocks and strengthened the regulatory outlook.

    Profitability is still meaningfully below year-ago levels, due in part to costs associated with going public over the summer, as well as the scaling up of the tokenization business at an active time for the entire sector, Securitize CEO Carlos Domingo told CNBC in an exclusive interview.

    It has been revealed that securitize reinforced "certain areas of the manufacturer like finance, compliance, legal [and] cybersecurity," which increased corporate costs "compared to a year ago when we were privately held," Domingo remarked. "We're in in a very good position. The adjusted EBITDA … is improving significantly from previous quarters.".

    Sources indicate that securitize reported an adjusted EBITDA loss of $2 million, compared with positive adjusted EBITDA of $3.6 million a year ago, better than a $5.5 million loss in the second quarter. The manufacturer posted a 183% increase in operating costs and expenses.

    It has been revealed that also on Monday, the Securitize board authorized a $50 million share buyback and confirmed the acquisition of River One, an institutional asset-backed financing platform developing technology to connect stablecoin capital with traditional lending markets. Terms were not disclosed.

    Securitize sees an opportunity to modernize the $9 trillion market for asset backed finance by using stablecoins to finance real world assets, generate yield and tokenize investment positions and credit products, Domingo remarked.The acquisition also marks an expansion beyond Securitize's core niche markets at a time when tokenization's competitive landscape is growing, with traditional asset managers like BlackRock and Franklin Templeton, and established financial market infrastructure providers like DTCC and Broadridge, entering the industry.

    "We have been very active in tokenized funds, treasuries [and] yield … And we've been obviously recently very active in tokenized stocks, so this adds another piece of the puzzle in the emerging tokenization space for us to capture revenue growth.".

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER.
    • Published: 17:30 EST, 15 November 2026 | Updated: 17:30 EST, 15 November 2026.
    • Sebastien Pocognoli has conceded that he doesn’t have 18 months to demonstrate that Scotland are on the right track under him.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER.

    Published: 17:30 EST, 15 November 2026 | Updated: 17:30 EST, 15 November 2026.

    Sebastien Pocognoli has conceded that he doesn’t have 18 months to demonstrate that Scotland are on the right track under him.

    Appointed Steve Clarke’s successor in the summer, the Belgian’s attempts to bring in fresh faces and a new style of play has produced mixed results in his opening five Nations League games.

    Following Friday’s win over North Macedonia, John McGinn warned the Tartan Army that it could take as long as 18 months for everything to click into place.

    But ahead of the final group match in St Gallen tomorrow evening, the manager acknowledged it’s incumbent on him to accelerate that time frame.

    Asked if he felt he had to deliver sooner, he said: ‘Yeah, for sure, but we’re only talking about 18 months because John said that. He could have said 15 months. I don’t know. But, for sure, it needs to be quicker.

    According to recent reports, ‘In 18 months, it will be the time of the Euros and that is what he meant. We have to go there and be prepared for this in 18 months’ time.

    Sebastien Pocognoli  states his Scotland team need to show progress 'game after game'.

    ‘For sure, game after game, we need to see improvement.

    It has been revealed that ‘Some fresh faces will come back in March. So, step by step we will have more ideas and in one month’s time a lot can change also.’.

    McGinn also noted that the players were fully behind the manager, reiterating the point previously made by Andy Robertson and Scott McTominay.

    ‘I can tell you that in the time we have had together the players have been doing well in terms of replicating what I ask them to do,’ the manager stressed.

    ‘They know that and that’s the most important part.

    ‘They buy in. They like it. I think they enjoy it too. You can see when players don’t enjoy it.

    ‘For sure, when you win it’s more enjoyable, but it would be very bad if they weren’t enjoying it and we were also not winning games.

    ‘So, right now I think we are working well. We give special attention to the collective.

    According to recent reports, ‘In all the camps, I am very clear about what I expect on the pitch. The players wanted this when I arrived. They wanted clarity. And I think that’s what I have tried to bring.’.

    To claim second place in the group, Scotland need to defeat the Swiss and hope that Slovenia don’t win in North Macedonia.

    That outcome would ensure that Pocognoli’s men would be a pot two side in next month’s Euro 2028 draw.

    Asked what it would take to pull off what would be a stunning win in St Gallen, the manager said: ‘Let’s be brave, but be intelligent.

    Recent findings suggest that ‘It’s about mentality. They (Switzerland) are a very good team, so we need to be smart. Sometimes they will go through our lines with a low block or a high block as they have the quality.

    ‘We will try to be intense and strong in the duel because I think that’s the first piece to have a good game.’.

    Pocognoli’s side were booed off at half-time on Friday with criticism of the performance persisting despite them going on to win the game.

    But the manager claims he’s oblivious to wider concerns about the performances to date, saying: ‘No, I’m not aware of this. That’s why I was surprised (at the question).

    John McGinn suggested that it could take 18 months for Scotland to click under Pocognoli.

    Industry observers note that ‘Yes, there were some boos at half-time. I think that’s part of it, it’s been like this for years.

    ‘I know we are colleagues, but I’m not reading the press.

    It has been revealed that ‘So, I’m not aware of the criticism. I just want to make the supporters happy.

    ‘If they aren’t yet happy, we will try to do better.

    According to recent reports, ‘There’s pressure in all the jobs with a club. It can be external, it can be internal. It is part of the job.

    ‘I’m very self-critical about myself. So, that’s the first thing. Try to be stable when we win, when we lose.

    ‘I’m always thinking what we can do better. If there’s some criticism, that’s fine.

    ‘But there there were also a lot of positives after the North Macedonia game.

    ‘I was the first one to say calm down as we need to see more.’.

    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    What's ahead for AI financing after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang departs

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (745 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure hasn't produced a broad shock to the credit market, but it is putting the tech giant's role as a financier of artificial intelligence infrastructure under scrutiny.
    • Huang, who stepped down Thursday amid an espionage and adultery scandal, built Nvidia into an AI powerhouse in the 33 years since he co-founded the company.
    • It has been revealed that nvidia not only supplies its graphics processing units to hyperscalers and tech giants, it also provides financing to other companies to help the industry expand.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure hasn't produced a broad shock to the credit market, but it is putting the tech giant's role as a financier of artificial intelligence infrastructure under scrutiny.

    Huang, who stepped down Thursday amid an espionage and adultery scandal, built Nvidia into an AI powerhouse in the 33 years since he co-founded the company. Chief financial officer Colette Kress has been named interim CEO as the company searches for a permanent chief executive.

    It has been revealed that nvidia not only supplies its graphics processing units to hyperscalers and tech giants, it also provides financing to other companies to help the industry expand. That could all change.

    "Although we expect the organization to fulfill all of its previously unveiled commitments, we believe that going forward, it may be more difficult for the company to negotiate fresh multi-party investments among ecosystem partners at the same scale it has done up to this point," Goldman Sachs analyst James Schneider said in a note Thursday.

    The news of Huang's resignation comes after investors were already concerned about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure.

    Sources indicate that tech bond yields have risen and spreads have widened on credit default swaps, most notably in lower-rated names. Credit default swaps are contracts in which investors pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. Wider spreads indicate investors view the bonds as riskier.

    On Friday, the yield on Nvidia's 4.5% bond due in 2031 sat at 5.717%, nearly 5% higher week to date. Bond yields move inversely to prices.

    Tech stocks slumped Friday with the Nasdaq 100 closing down 1.2% as markets continued to digest the Nvidia news. Yields on hyperscaler bonds ticked slightly higher on Friday, signaling the broader concern about AI debt lingers.

    It's the smaller AI companies that could ultimately see an impact if Nvidia makes any changes to its AI financing. The company had $36 billion in off-balance-sheet AI cloud agreements, or backstops, for neoclouds, according to its last quarterly financial filing in July.

    Recent findings suggest that neoclouds CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN are all in Nvidia's portfolio. Their shares were down sharply Thursday.

    Recent findings suggest that coreWeave, which has become the poster child for AI debt fears, saw its bond yields retreat after its quarterly earnings on Tuesday eased investor concerns. The yield on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 was 14.79% on Friday after climbing to 16.7% last week. The spread on its five-year CDS also dropped more than 17% week to date, although it remained above 1,000 — which is generally considered a sign of distress.

    It remains unclear how Nvidia's support for those companies may change, said CreditSights analyst Andy Li.

    "We don't know what the ultimate strategy for Nvidia is going to be coming out the other side," he remarked.

    "However, I think directionally, just given the fact that Jensen was so crucial in selling the Nvidia story and being a very aggressive deal maker, it's likely that a lot of this creative deal-making and circular financing and equity and credit support is going to moderate," he added.

    CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator told CNBC Wednesday, before Huang's departure, that Nvidia "is not one person.".

    In a recent development, "There are thousands of people over there that interface with thousands of people at my tech giant every day. They integrate on the technology. They integrate on the physical infrastructure. They integrate on the networking," he said in an interview with "Squawk on the Street." "They have been a great partner for us for years. They will continue to be a great partner for us.".

    Bob Lang, founder and chief strategist at Explosive Options, doesn't see any massive changes in terms of Nvidia's relevance or its ability to finance for now. As CFO, Kress was involved in the financing deals, and the search for a permanent CEO is going to take some time, he noted.

    The real issue is just how much money the tech giant will want to lend for AI financing, rather than, say using its hundreds of billions in free cash flow for other purposes, like share buybacks, capex, or acquisitions.

    "Big companies like Nvidia and Meta, they're holding all the cards," he said. "When they decide that the game is over, that's it — it's going to be curtains for some of these smaller companies.".

    — CNBC'S Kif Leswing and Isabel O'Brien contributed reporting.

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1287 w)

    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    Why Anthropic's blockbuster IPO couldn't escape the stock market correction

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1287 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that no one can say the Anthropic initial public offering wasn't a success for the organization.
    • The Anthropic IPO reinforces those fears rather than running counter to them, claims Avery Marquez, director of investment strategies at Renaissance Capital, which researches IPOs and manages the Renaissance IPO ETF (IPO).
    • "The volatility in the AI trade we've been seeing for the past few months stems from valuations and whether we are in a bubble, and that's been heightened and highlighted by the Anthropic IPO," Marquez stated on "ETF Edge" on Friday.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that no one can say the Anthropic initial public offering wasn't a success for the organization. Deal size and pricing were signs of what IPO experts say was insatiable demand for "ANT" shares. But what came within a day is something that investors better get used to: anxiety in the stock market about valuations being assigned to artificial intelligence revenue and business models that should keep Anthropic shares volatile in the period ahead.

    The Anthropic IPO reinforces those fears rather than running counter to them, claims Avery Marquez, director of investment strategies at Renaissance Capital, which researches IPOs and manages the Renaissance IPO ETF (IPO).

    "The volatility in the AI trade we've been seeing for the past few months stems from valuations and whether we are in a bubble, and that's been heightened and highlighted by the Anthropic IPO," Marquez stated on "ETF Edge" on Friday.

    And in the case of Anthropic, which finished trading Friday down 9%, the valuation anxiety becomes "so much more prevalent," she added, because it is a newly introduced stock.

    Industry observers note that it is not just any new stock, but one that has Wall Street adding downside risks to research notes likely never seen before, and which may be the greatest understatement (or most subtle equities research joke) in the history of earnings analysis. "Anthropic could develop AI systems which become fully autonomous and wipe out humanity which may lead to a serious decline in earnings," Seaport Research Partners analyst wrote Jay Goldberg wrote on Nov. 18.

    "It was challenging firm to value ... and it's very richly valued," Marquez mentioned. "We're seeing something more reasonable and investors grappling now with where should this company actually be valued," she added.

    Recent findings suggest that the fact that Anthropic pulled off the deal in this market and was able to command the price it did was an achievement, according to Yuri Khodjamirian, chief investment officer at Tema ETFs, which offers multiple funds that invest in pre-IPO shares of companies and held Anthropic in its Tema Photonics & Optical ETF (LAZR) well before IPO day. "We have to remember they pulled off a very large IPO in the middle of a very severe market with the volatility in the tech sector specifically," Khodjamirian stated on "ETF Edge.".

    Khodjamirian states the investor demand for AI remains, but amid a reassessment of returns. And he says an equally hard task has now begun for Anthropic. Investors are unwinding positions in everything from tech stocks to gold and bitcoin, and repositioning for 2027 based on their upcoming outlooks. "We are in a bit of vacuum," he remarked.

    Recent findings suggest that "From here on the market is trying trying to figure out what direction to go in," Khodjamirian remarked, whether that is based on Fed policy, geopolitics, the midterm elections results, or the AI trade. "In many cases, the chief investment officers I speak to, and the clients, say 'I'm just gonna take some risk off and wait and see until I get more info.' And with the Anthropic, the revenue picture and how the AI adoption curve progresses will be a vital stat to watch," he added.

    Sources indicate that plenty of value has already been wiped out in tech, according to Khodjamirian, but investors need newly introduced signals to buy. That doesn't just go for Anthropic but for much of the market's tech leadership. "One of the things most difficult for investors to understand right now is some of the leadership in the market that has been taken by semiconductor companies," he said, adding that the peak was 22% of S&P 500 earnings. But these companies, like Nvidia and Micron, have a very different earnings profile from the rest of the market.

    Industry observers note that the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH), which was down over 10% on Friday and around 15% for the week, was on pace for its worst week since September 2001, according to CNBC data on Friday afternoon. It also lost 15% in one week of March 2020. The tech sector of the S&P 500, tracked by the State Street Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLK), turned in its worst weekly performance since the Covid crash.

    Khodjamirian mentioned while these stocks may look cheap on a P/E basis right now after the heavy selling, that requires faith in the earnings estimates, which he says will be more important as results are released for the next few years. "Right now it looks cheap, but will companies like Micron and Nvidia actually deliver?".

    Nvidia shares fell 14% on Friday, adding to its worst stretch of weekly performance since 2008. What's more, the single biggest trade in the options market on Friday was a near $100-million bet that the VanEck Semiconductor ETF has a long way more to fall.

    And the same caution about the outlook goes for Anthropic, he remarked. "That's why we need to watch Anthropic's annual recurring revenue number, because it is a key part of puzzle," he said.

    Marquez said there is always hype in names like SpaceX and Anthropic when they go public, and it is hard to know whether the pricing of the deal is based on fundamentals, "but we just need more time and lots price discovery," she said. "It is not going to happen overnight," she added.

    As an IPO researcher, she says this "discernment" is a healthy thing for the markets. There are few cases to look to as comps for Anthropic, other than SpaceX, and before that, way back to Facebook's IPO in 2012. And neither example is one of quick recovery. SpaceX shares remain well below their first-day closing price more than five months after its IPO. Facebook (now Meta), meanwhile, "did not do well for the first year after going public and we see where it is now. It's just the nature of these disruptive tech companies that come to market," Marquez said. "They lend themselves to more volatility and a longer period of price discovery for investors.".

    Industry observers note that all eyes will next be on Anthropic's rival OpenAI, which has suggested it will be ready to go public in 2027. Marquez stated the reaction to the Anthropic deal may be a signal that it was "a good idea to wait, allowing themselves to build more quarters of better financials and improve fundamentals a bit before taking on a market that is really quite discerning.".

    Tema does not own shares of OpenAI in any of its ETFs. But, "I can't say it wont be," Khodjamirian remarked. "They exist out there in the secondary market, and we will look at it, but we haven't made any decision. It depends on the ETF fit and if the portfolio manager wants to invest. We are always looking out for these interesting businesses but never just for the sake of private exposure," he added.

    It has been revealed that tema does own Databricks, Stripe, Kalshi and Polymarket across its funds. It also was an investor in SpaceX pre-IPO through its Tema Space Innovators ETF (NASA).

    Khodjamirian said demand from public market investors to access these "generational businesses" will continue to be the case, despite the market volatility, and will more often come before IPO day. In fact, he pointed to the filing from the world's largest asset manager and one of the biggest ETF companies in the world, BlackRock, earlier this week. It wants to bring out a fresh kind of exchange-traded product that would bring the ETF and interval fund structures together as a way to increase exposure to private companies, with shares trading on an exchange while the fund makes monthly repurchase offers.

    General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    An early breakdown in the polar vortex is threatening already depleted gas stocks

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (755 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • An unprecedented early breakdown of the stratospheric polar vortex and a record-breaking El Niño event has put energy traders on alert this winter, with analysts warning the weather and climate phenomena could have an outsized impact on Europe.
    • Meteorologists are currently observing a record early breakdown of the polar vortex, a large-scale circulation of strong winds that typically keeps extremely cold air over the North Pole.
    • Changes in the strength and shape of the polar vortex can influence weather patterns much lower down in the atmosphere, potentially bringing in colder weather to parts of Europe and North America.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    An unprecedented early breakdown of the stratospheric polar vortex and a record-breaking El Niño event has put energy traders on alert this winter, with analysts warning the weather and climate phenomena could have an outsized impact on Europe.

    Meteorologists are currently observing a record early breakdown of the polar vortex, a large-scale circulation of strong winds that typically keeps extremely cold air over the North Pole.

    Changes in the strength and shape of the polar vortex can influence weather patterns much lower down in the atmosphere, potentially bringing in colder weather to parts of Europe and North America.

    This year, however, the collapse of the stratospheric polar vortex, or SPV, is taking place at the same time as an unusually powerful El Niño, a climate event that can boost global temperatures and disrupt rainfall.

    The collision of these two events raises the risk of a prolonged cold spell that could lift heating demand and force European countries to draw down already-low reserves faster. That would leave the continent more reliant on imported liquefied natural gas (LNG) at a time when supplies from the Middle East are disrupted.

    To be sure, Europe's natural gas storage levels started the winter at their lowest level in more than a decade.

    The International Energy Agency warned earlier this month that low European storage levels and limited storage options in several LNG-importing countries in Asia and South America could intensify the competition for cargoes and put upward pressure on prices during periods of high demand.

    Simon Lee, a lecturer in atmospheric science at the U.K.'s University of St Andrews, said the combination of a sudden stratospheric warming (SSW) with an El Niño event is not necessarily unusual, but meteorologists had been expecting a polar vortex breakdown in February — not as early as November.

    The early SPV disruption is an "extremely rare" event that could influence winter weather in northwest Europe and the eastern U.S., Lee said, increasing the chance of colder conditions although likely not to the extent that a polar vortex event caused parts of Niagara Falls to partially freeze in January 2014.

    "Geopolitics and weather are the two key volatility drives for energy and now they seem to be happening at the same time — and that's always the biggest risk for markets," Florence Schmit, senior energy strategist at Rabobank, told CNBC.

    For months, meteorologists expected an El Niño event would result in a milder winter in Europe and relatively muted heating demand, Schmit noted, which was broadly seen as welcome news given ongoing concerns over the continent's tight regional supplies for gas and crude oil.

    In a recent development, the prospect of a colder-than-expected winter due to an early breakdown of the polar vortex could be "incredibly difficult" for Europe to navigate, Schmit warned. She noted that the region's gas storages have seen "very, very strong withdrawals" over the last two weeks, "which is quite unusual for this time of year.".

    It has been revealed that "If you continue to see the same storage withdrawals over the next couple of months, that means energy prices will spike again — and they won't spike because of geopolitics. This time it will be the weather driving that spike and that volatility," Schmit mentioned.

    European gas prices have soared to levels not seen since the 2022 energy crisis in recent weeks, notching 103.9 euros ($113.99) per megawatt hour in late October. European benchmark Dutch TTF futures for December delivery stood at around 87.28 euros on Friday afternoon.

    "We have never seen an early breakdown of the polar vortex and a super el Nino in the same winter so we have no historical precedent on how this will impact global gas demand," David Lewis, principal research analyst of gas and liquified natural gas at Wood Mackenzie, told CNBC by email.

    El Niño is commonly associated with milder winters, while a SSW event typically leads to colder temperatures and higher snowfall, Lewis said, noting this could materialize in December and January within Europe.

    "So far, the start of the European winter heating season has been quite cold but more importantly has seen low wind speeds across Northern Europe," Lewis said.

    Recent findings suggest that "The drawdown in stocks in the first half of November has been amongst the highest on record. With inventories starting the winter at their lowest level on record, any further deterioration in temperatures or wind speeds will have an outsized impact on European balances and lead to higher prices across Europe," he added.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • (See the video above for Frank's complete chart breakdown.).
    • Recent findings suggest that is the Nasdaq-100's recent bounce a sign that the bottom is in?

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (See the video above for Frank's complete chart breakdown.).

    Recent findings suggest that is the Nasdaq-100's recent bounce a sign that the bottom is in? We're going to look at several charts to help answer that question.

    First, let's remember how we got here. In September, the NDX broke out from a bullish cup-and-handle pattern, producing a 33,200-upside target. That breakout quickly failed, however, and gave way to a bearish pattern that broke down aggressively two weeks ago.

    The decline brought the index relatively close to its 26,350 downside target before the current rebound began.

    Zooming out, it's telling to see where the bounce originated. Three notable forms of support converged in the 25,000-26,000 area:.

    This confluence of support helped encourage buying after a roughly 15% decline.

    For perspective, we also see what larger drawdowns of 20%, 30%, 40%, and 50% would look like … a lot worse.

    The following chart tracks NDX drawdowns from 52-week highs going back to just after the financial crisis. Only a handful of declines exceeded 20%, and three produced relatively quick reversals: late 2018, the Covid lows in 2020 and April 2025.

    Historically, buying into declines of approximately 15%–25% has generally paid off, even when additional downside occurred first (yellow highlights).

    The chart also highlights previous declines of 10%–16% in green, putting the current pullback into perspective.

    The major exception was 2022, when the NDX eventually declined nearly 36% over approximately 10 months ... a much worse outcome, which many investors are concerned could happen again now.

    That raises the key question: Are we experiencing another routine correction, or the early stages of a larger bear market?

    One vital clue will be how far this bounce progresses.

    Any rally that fails to reclaim the previous highs could establish a significant lower high. Additional lower highs would provide stronger evidence of a developing, longer downtrend.

    We saw this in March 2022, when that first sharp rebound effort failed to reach the previous high before a much more severe decline followed.

    The bottom line: The current bounce is encouraging, particularly given where it originated and knowing how well buying prior 10-20% drawdowns has paid off.

    It has been revealed that from here, it's all about the follow through. We don't need to see new highs right away, but any rally from here that's met with another wave of strong selling could reignite downside momentum.

    #85060. A trading strategy to ride out the Nvidia uncertainty and generate income in the process

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (632 w)
    📖 Baca
    Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    A trading strategy to ride out the Nvidia uncertainty and generate income in the process

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (632 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation has sent shockwaves through the tech sector, dragging Nvidia's (NVDA) stock down roughly 30% since Oct.
    • Industry observers note that however, for opportunistic investors, this panic has made the stock cheaper (obviously) while options have become significantly more expensive.
    • Buying good companies at a discount is investing 101, but the current market dynamics may do something else for those who use options.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation has sent shockwaves through the tech sector, dragging Nvidia's (NVDA) stock down roughly 30% since Oct. 6. The market despises uncertainty, and losing a visionary founder, particularly one without a well-telegraphed succession proposal, makes it worse.

    Industry observers note that however, for opportunistic investors, this panic has made the stock cheaper (obviously) while options have become significantly more expensive. Trading in the $160s, Nvidia's valuation has taken a major haircut, yet its underlying business fundamentals remain largely intact. While Huang was the architect of Nvidia's AI dominance, the manufacturer's moat — superior GPUs, the CUDA software ecosystem, and networking expertise — does not walk out the door with him. The company's structural advantage in the global artificial intelligence rollout persists.

    Buying good companies at a discount is investing 101, but the current market dynamics may do something else for those who use options. Huang's departure guarantees that Nvidia will be operating under a cloud of transition for the foreseeable future. Executing a permanent CEO search while navigating global regulatory scrutiny takes time. Consequently, Nvidia's implied volatility (IV)—the market's pricing of expected future price swings — has spiked to highs not seen since the tariff tantrum in the first half of 2025, and this elevated IV is highly likely to persist for several months as the leadership drama slowly unfolds.

    According to recent reports, this prolonged period of high implied volatility can be a goldmine for option sellers, specifically those executing options overlays such as covered call strategies. When you buy NVDA shares at these depressed levels and simultaneously sell out-of-the-money call options against your position, the premiums you collect are directly tied to IV. Because fear and transition-related uncertainty have dramatically inflated these option prices, the income generated from selling covered calls is now significantly higher than usual.

    In a recent development, this lowers the risk profile of holding the stock considerably over time. Consistently collecting these inflated premiums systematically lowers your overall cost basis in the underlying shares. If the stock trades sideways or recovers slowly during the CEO search, you are generating an outsized cash yield on a stagnant asset. If the stock experiences further downside turbulence, the heavy premium income acts as a substantial downside buffer, meaningfully reducing the strategy's overall risk over time.

    By deploying a persistent covered call strategy, investors can leverage the exact fear driving the stock down to generate robust, risk-reducing income while maintaining exposure to the undeniable future of AI.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that zscaler shares surged 18% in extended trading on Friday after Bloomberg reported that CrowdStrike is in talks to buy the cybersecurity vendor. Shares of CrowdStrike shares fell more than 8%.

    The talks between the two companies are ongoing, Bloomberg reported, citing sources familiar in the matter. CrowdStrike declined to comment on the report. Zscaler didn't immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.

    CrowdStrike has been one of the big cybersecurity winners in the artificial intelligence boom, with its stock about doubling in value this year, lifting its market cap to $235 billion. Zscaler, meanwhile, is down 13% this year, pushing its market cap down to about $32 billion.

    Along with CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Networks has seen its business boom as businesses race to upgrade their networks in the AI era. Palo Alto closed Friday at a nearly $282 billion market cap.

    Industry observers note that should a deal take place, it would be among the largest in the history of the cybersecurity industry. Google acquired Wiz last year for $32 billion. In 2024, Cisco paid about $28 billion for Splunk. Earlier this year, Palo Alto closed its purchase of CyberArk for $25 billion.

    CrowdStrike's deals to this point have been on the smaller side.The company announced prepares earlier this month to acquire agentic observability platform Fiddler AI and AI trust platform Dreadnode.

    #85054. I never wanted the American Dream and I felt like something was wrong with me—until I moved abroad

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1002 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    I never wanted the American Dream and I felt like something was wrong with me—until I moved abroad

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1002 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I got my first job at 17, working the register at an Eckerd's drugstore in Texas.
    • It has been revealed that it all felt suffocating: the added responsibility, the longer hours, the idea that this was the ladder I was supposed to want to climb.
    • I never wanted the American Dream I saw so many people around me striving to achieve.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I got my first job at 17, working the register at an Eckerd's drugstore in Texas. My manager was only a few years older than me, and while my coworkers seemed motivated by the idea of working their way up to his position, I felt no desire to follow that path.

    It has been revealed that it all felt suffocating: the added responsibility, the longer hours, the idea that this was the ladder I was supposed to want to climb. I wanted to work, but I couldn't wrap my head around building my whole identity around a job.

    I never wanted the American Dream I saw so many people around me striving to achieve. For a long time, I wondered if something was wrong with me. It wasn't until I finally made a long-term move abroad about a decade ago that I realized it was okay to want something different.

    After college, I got a job in travel sales. I was good at it. Talking about travel all day suited the wanderlust I'd carried since my first trip abroad in my teens.

    Industry observers note that I continued working in sales, marketing and the odd temp role for years. But they were always just jobs. I didn't feel like they defined me or feel a calling to an industry or title the way people around me seemed to.

    Industry observers note that of course, I wanted financial stability, but I was unwilling to sacrifice my time and well-being to get it. I just didn't connect with the version of ambition that meant grinding toward a corner office. What I wanted the most wasn't status; it was freedom, growth and new experiences.

    In a recent development, the wanderlust eventually caught up to me, and at 26 I moved to Spain to teach English. Even though I was working, people saw it as taking a year off from my career and warned me it could damage my resume. I simply didn't care. Living for my resume had never made sense to me.

    Looking back, I think being abroad offered an escape from the pressure to chase the traditional path of the American Dream. There, I felt free to enjoy life and figure out who I was without worrying about what box I needed to tick next.

    Industry observers note that I wanted to stay in Spain, but I couldn't find a visa that would let me live there long-term, so I returned to the U.S. I became a serial job hopper for almost 10 years, quitting a job every year to spend summers visiting friends in the Netherlands, the U.K. and Switzerland or solo traveling in Spain on the money I'd saved up.

    Sources indicate that on the personal side, I wasn't in a rush to get married or have kids. In my 30s, single and childfree, I felt like I was failing at adulthood, even though deep down, I didn't actually want the things I was supposedly behind on. Settling down just because everyone else was doing it never felt right to me.

    Recent findings suggest that and I couldn't shake the dream of living in Europe. In my 20s, people mostly assumed my desire to travel was a phase. By my 30s, the conversations had shifted and I was getting pulled aside. Friends, family and colleagues all had some version of the same message: It was time to get serious and build a life in Texas.

    But my gut said to try one more time. So I did.

    Industry observers note that in 2015, on my fourth attempt, I finally made it to Spain for good. It was scary to shake things up when everyone around me was settling down, but deep down I knew at 35, this was my chance to stop trying to conform and start building a life that felt right for me.

    In my new home, the pace was slower. I promptly noticed that people actually took their vacations. Strangers at a dinner party didn't immediately ask me what I did for work. Adults in their 30s, 40s and beyond were out living full social lives. Single, childfree women my age didn't feel like an anomaly.

    Living abroad didn't solve everything overnight. I still had to figure out how to support myself. But having the space to define myself professionally without constant judgment changed what felt possible.

    In 2017, I launched She Hit Refresh, where I help women over 30 figure out how to move to Europe and build upcoming lives for themselves. It's not something I could have created from anywhere else, with any other experience than my own.

    In the process, I've met so many others who left corporate America behind to create something different for themselves. I've seen more women asking the same questions I spent years asking myself. Burnt out, disillusioned with hustle culture, realizing that checking all the boxes of the American Dream they grew up on didn't deliver the feeling they were promised.

    Industry observers note that we're all figuring it out together; each of us writing a version of a life that didn't fit a standard template. Moving abroad helped me understand that success, for me, was never about earning more or owning more. It was always about more ease, more time, more space, more life.

    Industry observers note that for years, I thought I was behind. I felt like something was wrong with me for wanting a different kind of life. Looking back, I just hadn't found my place yet.

    Sources indicate that cepee Tabibian is the founder of She Hit Refresh, where she's helped over 24,000 women age 30+ plan their move abroad. Grab her free Move Abroad After 30 Guide to start planning your own move. The daughter of Colombian and Iranian immigrants, Cepee grew up in Houston, Texas, before becoming an immigrant herself in Spain. Follow her @shehitrefresh.

    📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1107 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: Berkshire breaks out to record high with fourth-quarter rally reaching 19%

    📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1107 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Berkshire Hathaway's red-hot shares are ending a strong week with four consecutive fresh record high closes.
    • Since the rally began with the start of the fourth quarter on October 1, the Class A shares have closed at record highs 11 times as they soared 19.1%.
    • The much more widely held B shares closed at new highs just 10 times but are also up 19.1% from their near-term low.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Berkshire Hathaway's red-hot shares are ending a strong week with four consecutive fresh record high closes.

    Since the rally began with the start of the fourth quarter on October 1, the Class A shares have closed at record highs 11 times as they soared 19.1%.

    The much more widely held B shares closed at new highs just 10 times but are also up 19.1% from their near-term low.

    The gains are in sharp contrast to the S&P 500's 1.2% dip as investors appear to be seeing Berkshire as a relatively safe haven amid worries about AI stocks and spending.

    Both Berkshire classes were up 3.9% on the week as the S&P advanced by 2.5%, its best week since early August.

    Berkshire's B shares are now 7.5 percentage points ahead of the benchmark for the year so far.

    After erasing their post-Buffett CEO announcement losses three weeks ago, Berkshire shares are now up almost 10% since last year's shareholders meeting.

    They've gained around 29% since last August's lows and are up around 18% year-to-date.

    Berkshire Hathaway is due to disclose its quarterly equity portfolio snapshot on Monday when it files its Q3 13F with the SEC.

    We won't know for sure until then, but numbers in the firm's third quarter 10-Q, released last Saturday, indicate Berkshire continued to reduce its Bank of America stake.

    It would be the ninth consecutive quarter of selling.

    As of June 30, Berkshire reported holding 483.4 million BAC shares valued now at $24.7 billion, it's fifth largest equity position.

    On June 30, 2024, before the selling began, Berkshire owned just over 1 billion shares valued at $41.1 billion.

    Since then, the number of shares in the portfolio has decreased by 53.2%, not including any Q3 sales, while the stock price has increased by 28.3%.

    If there had been no reductions, the position would be worth $52.7 billion.

    The belief Berkshire sold more BAC shares in the third quarter is based on a $372 million reduction in the cost basis for equities categorized by the company as "banks, insurance, and finance.".

    The 10-Q also reports $2.2 billion of pretax gains from equity sales.

    Barron's notes Bank of America and American Express are the only financial stocks in the portfolio that have a cost basis low enough to generate a gain like that. Amex is one of the four stocks upcoming CEO Greg Abel indicated would be held for "decades" to come in his February letter to shareholders.

    In any case, Berkshire's almost 23% stake in Amex would have required it to promptly disclose any sales.

    Based on the numbers in the 10-Q, the warrants Berkshire received as part of a 2011 $5 billion investment in the bank that it used in 2017 to buy 700 million shares at $7.14 each, and BAC's average stock price in the quarter, Barron's estimates 30 to 40 million shares may have been sold.

    That would be roughly in line with the 30.2 million shares sold in the second quarter.

    Sources indicate that the case isn't as good, but Barron's thinks Berkshire may have bought more Alphabet shares in the period. That's based on a $2.3 billion increase in the cost basis for the category that includes Google's parent.

    Overall, it looks like it will be a relatively quiet quarter with $2.4 billion in equity purchases and $2.8 billion in sales.

    According to recent reports, in the first quarter, Berkshire bought $15.9 billion and sold $24.1 billion of equities. In the second quarter, it purchased $23.5 billion and sold $3.7 billion.

    All those numbers exclude the company's buybacks of its own stock.

    In a term sheet filed early Friday, Berkshire Hathaway says it is selling more than 182 billion yen ($1.1 billion) worth of bonds with maturities between 2029 and 2056 and annual interest rates between 2.6% and 4.6%.

    Bloomberg points out the rates, compared to benchmarks, are higher than its previous sale this year.

    It quotes a fund manager as saying market sentiment "has become more sensitive," forcing issuers to make their offerings more attractive.

    In April, Berkshire sold 272 billion yen ($1.7 billion) of bonds.

    Berkshire uses the proceeds from the yen-denominated bonds to protect its ongoing investments in Japanese stocks from currency fluctuations.

    Some links may require a subscription:.

    Warren Buffett recommends Benjamin Graham's book, "The Intelligent Investor," and outlines what he considers Graham's three most vital ideas.

    WARREN BUFFETT: On investment books, if you're asking about that, I would recommend the first two books that Phil Fisher wrote back around 1960, "Common Sense [Stocks] and Uncommon Profits" and the second one ["Paths to Wealth Through Common Stocks"]. They're very good books.

    You know, I obviously recommend, first and foremost, [Benjamin Graham's] "The Intelligent Investor," with chapters eight and 20 are the ones that you really should read.

    Two of the — well, all of the key ideas in investing, really, are in that book, because there's only about three ideas. And those — two of them are emphasized in those two chapters...

    One is that — to think of yourself — to think of investing as owning a business and not buying something that wiggles around in price.

    And the second one is your attitude, which ties in with that, the attitude toward the market, that's covered in chapter eight. And if you have the proper attitude toward market movements, it's an enormous help in securities.

    And the final chapter is on the margin of safety, which means, don't try and drive a 9,800-pound truck over a bridge that states it's, you know, "Capacity: 10,000 pounds." But go down the road a little bit and find one that says, "Capacity: 15,000 pounds.".

    #85050. Breaking: Retirees face a looming deadline for required withdrawals — missing it could trigger a tax penalty

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (649 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Retirees face a looming deadline for required withdrawals — missing it could trigger a tax penalty

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (649 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, every year, millions of Americans must take required withdrawals from retirement accounts by Dec.
    • Amid the busy holiday season, it's easy to miss the year-end deadline for required minimum distributions — a mistake that can trigger a hefty IRS penalty, experts remarked.
    • "One of the most common RMD mistakes is waiting until the last minute," mentioned certified financial planner Alex Canellopoulos, director of wealth at Vista Capital Partners in Portland, Oregon.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, every year, millions of Americans must take required withdrawals from retirement accounts by Dec. 31.

    Amid the busy holiday season, it's easy to miss the year-end deadline for required minimum distributions — a mistake that can trigger a hefty IRS penalty, experts remarked.

    "One of the most common RMD mistakes is waiting until the last minute," mentioned certified financial planner Alex Canellopoulos, director of wealth at Vista Capital Partners in Portland, Oregon.

    Most retirees must start RMDs from pretax accounts at age 73. The withdrawal is based on the previous year's account balances on Dec. 31, your age and an IRS "life expectancy factor.".

    Sources indicate that the first annual RMD deadline is April 1 of the year after you turn 73, and future withdrawals are due by Dec. 31. If you wait until April 1 for the first one, you'll need two RMDs that year.

    RMDs also apply to certain inherited IRAs if the original IRA owner reached RMD age before their death.

    Recent findings suggest that in 2023, more than 14.8 million taxpayers age 70 or older had a traditional individual retirement account, according to the latest IRS data. The average year-end market value of the accounts was about $330,000.

    Deferring RMDs until the last minute raises the likelihood of mistakes, such as overlooking certain retirement accounts or making withdrawal calculation errors, Canellopoulos stated.

    Some 7% of Vanguard investors at RMD age missed their yearly withdrawal in 2025, up slightly from 6.7% in 2024, according to a Vanguard analysis of about 400,000 RMD-age retirees with IRA balances published in December 2025.

    Among those investors, the average missed RMD was $10,500 in 2025, Vanguard told CNBC.

    Investors who don't take RMDs by the annual deadline may owe an excise tax to the IRS, worth up to 25% of the amount they should have withdrawn. For example, the excise tax could be up to $2,625 for a $10,500 missed RMD.

    If investors miss a required withdrawal, they could reduce the penalty to 10% if they "timely corrected" the RMD within two years and file Form 5329, according to the IRS.

    It has been revealed that in some cases, the IRS could waive the penalty entirely due to "reasonable error" if investors take "reasonable steps" to fix the shortfall, according to the agency. Investors can file Form 5329 with a letter of explanation to request the waiver.

    Sources indicate that "If you don't ask, you're not going to get it," mentioned certified public accountant Tim Steffen, director of advanced planning at financial services firm Baird. "I've never heard of anybody being denied the waiver.".

    Investors who give to charity may be skipping a specific donation strategy that can reduce or eliminate their annual RMDs, according to Lawrence Pon, a CFP and CPA based in Redwood City, California.

    They can use a so-called qualified charitable distribution, or QCD, Pon mentioned.

    A QCD has a dual tax benefit: It doesn't count as taxable income and may also satisfy at least part of an investor's yearly RMD, Pon said.

    Industry observers note that the move requires a direct transfer from an investor's pretax IRA to an eligible nonprofit organization. They can donate up to $111,000 in 2026. While QCD eligibility begins at age 70½, transfers won't start counting toward RMDs until an investor reaches their RMD age.

    Sources indicate that generally, taxpayers only get a tax break for large charitable donations if they itemize deductions on their tax returns. But QCDs still provide a tax benefit for charitable gifts when investors use the standard deduction.

    QCDs "provide a real benefit if you are not itemizing [tax deductions]," said Pon.

    While there's no tax deduction for QCDs, the transfer won't increase a taxpayer's adjusted gross income, or AGI. Raising AGI can cause other tax consequences, such as higher premiums for Medicare Part B and Part D.

    #85048. Week 13 College Football Rankings: Texas, Tennessee Rise Amid Catastrophic Fall for UCLA, Indiana After Week 12

    Week 13 College Football Rankings: Texas, Tennessee Rise Amid Catastrophic Fall for UCLA, Indiana After Week 12

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 26 min read (5270 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Yahoo
